items.title: European Central Bank keeps key interest rate on hold at 2.5%
items.summary: Markets saw the decision as a hawkish pause and were last pricing in a 67% chance of a December rate hike.
items.body: The European Central Bank voted to hold interest rates steady on Thursday, meeting market expectations, despite euro zone inflation rising to a three-year high. It keeps the central bank's key rate, the deposit facility, at 2.5% following a 25 basis point hike in September . In a statement, the institution's Governing Council said rising energy prices posed upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to growth, but that underlying inflation and wages were so far broadly stable. "At this point in time we are not seeing second round effects in addition to what is already included in the projections" released in September, ECB President Christine Lagarde told CNBC's Annette Weisbach during a press conference.

items.title: Coinbase net income surges 66% in third quarter, benefiting from bitcoin investment gains
items.summary: Coinbase posted better-than-expected earnings in the third quarter, largely due to a recovery in the cryptocurrency market.
items.body: Coinbase Global earned third-quarter adjusted net income of $719 million , up 66% from $433 million a year ago, largely due to a recovery in the cryptocurrency market. Coinbase said it earned $2.51 a share in the latest quarter, although it wasn't immediately clear if that compared with the 6-cent-per-share profit that Wall Street analysts had estimated. Revenue of $1.20 billion trailed the $1.233 billion expected by analysts polled by LSEG. Net income at the San Francisco-based platform surged thanks to the value of its volatile cryptocurrency investment portfolio, which can swing wildly even when the composition of the underlying holdings are little changed. The third quarter value of Coinbase's crypto investment portfolio climbed due to a resurgence in the digital asset market.

items.title: Google value plunges by $500bn as AI fears rattle Wall Street
items.summary: Google spooked investors so badly that its stock hit a six-month low, after it revealed its AI search summaries were affecting ad revenue.
items.body: Google parent Alphabet lost just over $500bn (£374bn) in value on Thursday after it rattled Wall Street with its last update of the year on its business operations. Google spooked investors so badly that its stock hit a six-month low, after it revealed its artificial intelligence (AI) summaries on search were affecting ad revenue. Microsoft and Amazon also updated investors this week, and joined Google in plans to keep spending astronomical sums of cash in an ongoing AI race. But investors appeared dismayed at the impacts these plans are having on the ability of each to keep growing their core lines of business. At first glance, the quarterly results of Alphabet, the parent company of Google, were not at all bad. Total revenue grew 25% compared to last year, hitting $127.6bn. It was buoyed by the ongoing success of Google Cloud, where revenue grew by 103% to almost $31bn.

items.title: Healey’s budget paves way for ‘brutal’ spending review next year, warns IFS
items.summary: Thinktank says chancellor has given himself a mountain to climb after ducking big decisions in low-key speech John Healey has paved the way for a “brutal” spending review next year after his budget failed to cover a £28bn shortfall in the public finances needed to avoid a return…
items.body: John Healey has paved the way for a “brutal” spending review next year after his budget failed to cover a £28bn shortfall in the public finances needed to avoid a return to austerity, according to Britain’s leading tax and spending experts. A day after his address to the Commons , the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the chancellor had left himself a mountain to climb by ducking several big decisions in his debut tax and spending statement. After his low-key speech designed with febrile bond markets in mind, the thinktank said Healey had left plans for overall departmental spending across the rest of the parliament broadly unchanged in cash terms. But as the war in the Middle East fuels a surge in inflation – raising the cost of delivering public services – the chancellor has in effect pencilled in large cuts in the run-up to the next general election.

items.title: India increases growth forecast for fiscal year
items.summary: India's Ministry of Finance has increased its growth forecasts for the current fiscal year. But it also warned about inflation, particularly for fuel and energy, amid continued instability in the Middle East.
items.body: India's Ministry of Finance expects India's economy to grow at a pace of 7.3% in the current fiscal year based on its latest assessment of current data, it said in its October economic review . India's current fiscal year, known as FY27, runs from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027. The report contrasted these figures with global growth predictions of nearer 3%, saying "India's growth momentum, by comparison, has held firm." The ministry said growth in various key indicators like energy consumption, port traffic, goods and services tax (GST) collections, and car sales had accelerated in the previous quarter. However, the ministry also warned of continued inflationary pressure and pressure on the rupee currency, as well as downside risks from the El Nino weather phonemenon that could threaten soil moisture ahead of the winter sowing season.

items.title: Piero Cipollone: Next-day securities settlement, tokenisation and the transformation of Europe’s financial infrastructure
items.body: Less than a year from now, on 11 October 2027, Europe will move to T+1 settlement. This means that the time from the moment a security is traded to the moment the buyer receives it and the seller is paid will be reduced from two days to one. The transition to T+1 is part of a broader transformation of Europe’s financial infrastructure. And the objective is clear: to make Europe’s financial and payment system more efficient, more resilient and safer, and ultimately to make European financial markets more competitive. In the Eurosystem, we are contributing to this transformation across the full spectrum of our mandate. These are not separate projects. They are different parts of the same strategy: ensuring that the euro and Europe’s financial markets are fit for the future in a rapidly changing world. It is about more than just reducing the time between trade and settlement to one day.

items.title: China slams EU’s potential new trade safeguards, says they may violate WTO rules
items.summary: Beijing reiterated its opposition on Thursday to potential new European Union trade safeguards targeting Chinese exports, vowing to take “all necessary measures” to defend the interests of its companies. “Artificially restricting normal trade is suspected of violating World…
items.body: Beijing reiterated its opposition on Thursday to potential new European Union trade safeguards targeting Chinese exports, vowing to take “all necessary measures” to defend the interests of its companies. “Artificially restricting normal trade is suspected of violating World Trade Organization rules,” said Huang Ling, spokeswoman for China’s Ministry of Commerce, at a weekly press conference. “Far from improving the competitiveness of EU industry, it will increase the burden on downstream industries, push up inflation in the EU, and undermine the security and stability of global industrial and supply chains.” Huang was responding to reports that Brussels is considering rolling out broader safeguards – including tariffs and import quotas – to stem a flood of Chinese imports, as the European Union steps up efforts to narrow its widening trade deficit with China.

items.title: Alphabet tanks nearly 13% for worst day ever, losing $500 billion in value
items.summary: Alphabet reported a larger negative free cash flow than analysts had expected while maintaining its spending gudiance for the year.
items.body: Alphabet shares plunged the most since Google went public in 2004, dropping 13% on Thursday, wiping out roughly $500 billion in market cap. In its earnings announcement late Wednesday, Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion for the third quarter, compared to the $2.7 billion analysts expected. The Google parent maintained its full year capital expenditure guidance of between $195 billion and $205 billion. Microsoft , meanwhile, traded largely flat as investors focused on the tech giants' latest spending and free cash flow numbers in the third-quarter earnings report. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, which was 30% higher than a year ago, but below analyst projections of $50.67 billion. Free cash flow fell 27% to $18.63 billion but remained positive.

items.body: TOKYO -- Japanese companies will be able to expand drone services after a cap on simultaneous operations by a single pilot were scrapped, potentially helping to fill gaps left by labor shortages.

items.title: Third-quarter U.S. GDP increases a better-than-expected 3.4% as September inflation accelerates
items.summary: The personal consumption expenditures price index was projected to increase 0.5% in September for an annual rate of 3.7%, according to the Dow Jones consensus.
items.body: The pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target, while the economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department reports Thursday. The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6%. The monthly increase was the largest since March but in line with the Dow Jones consensus, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below. Excluding food and energy, the core PCE posted respective readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, in line with the consensus. While the Fed follows both measures closely, officials generally see the core reading as more indicative of longer-term inflation trends.

items.title: Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse
items.summary: Poundland's bosses are filing a notice of intention to appoint administrators to the business.
items.body: Andy Burnham has said the government is "ready to support" Poundland staff as the retailer teeters on the brink of collapse. The prime minister called for answers over why an offer to buy the business from its current owners, which would have protected jobs, was rejected. "This is a deeply worrying time for Poundland staff and their families," Burnham told the BBC. The discount chain is teetering on the edge after its US-based owners Gordon Brothers cut off a vital funding supply and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG). Burnham said: "We want to see jobs protected. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn't been accepted, then the Business Secretary and I want to know why that is the case. The retailer's bosses have filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, giving the business 10 days to find a rescue deal.

items.title: Lloyds executive criticises Healey for linking bank tax rises to energy bill support
items.summary: Chief financial officer says he hopes budget measure is temporary as sector provides loans that fuel growth A senior Lloyds Banking Group executive has criticised the chancellor for linking bank tax increases to energy bill support for UK households, as he warned the government…
items.body: A senior Lloyds Banking Group executive has criticised the chancellor for linking bank tax increases to energy bill support for UK households, as he warned the government against extending the higher levy beyond March 2028. Lloyds’s chief financial officer, William Chalmers, acknowledged that the economic environment was “challenging” but said the government should not seek to ease pressure on households at the expense of the banking sector as it provides loans that could fuel UK growth. “Ultimately, it is important that the UK banking sector is able to deliver banking services to businesses and households and communities in a cost-effective way, in order to promote UK growth,” he said, adding that it was also important that the sector stayed internationally competitive.

items.title: Christine Lagarde, Boris Vujčić: Monetary policy statement (with Q&A)
items.body: The Governing Council today decided to keep the three key ECB interest rates unchanged. Energy prices have continued to rise, posing upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to the growth outlook. While the full effects of the energy shock are still unfolding, underlying inflation has remained broadly stable so far and wages do not show a material response at this stage. The increased magnitude and duration of the energy shock, as well as the implications for indirect and second-round effects, are likely to drive up inflation and lower growth. Financing conditions have tightened since our last meeting, which is likely to weigh on inflation and growth. We are committed to setting monetary policy to ensure that inflation stabilises at our two per cent target in the medium term. We remain well positioned to navigate the current elevated uncertainty.

items.title: China’s BYD, Geely report profit jump as sales abroad surge, though local market stalls

items.body: China’s two largest carmakers, BYD and Geely Auto, reported a jump in their third-quarter earnings, propelled by surging overseas sales as they intensified pressure on established international marques in Europe and Southeast Asia. BYD, mainland China’s largest automotive group, posted a net profit of 10 billion yuan (US$1.5 billion) in the three months ending September, up 28 per cent from the same period a year earlier. Revenue grew 13.6 per cent to 211.5 billion yuan. Geely said on Thursday that its net income between July and September climbed 28 per cent to 4.8 billion yuan, while revenue increased 10 per cent to 99 billion yuan. The third-quarter performances of both BYD and Geely failed to meet Bloomberg survey estimates.

items.title: The politics of President Lagarde's European Central Bank early exit — and who could replace her
items.summary: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will step down on Feb. 7 next year, she announced Thursday.
items.body: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will step down on Feb. 7 next year, she announced Thursday, formally kicking off a succession race that will be shaped by political bargaining and France's looming fiscal crisis. Lagarde has led the central bank since July 2019, steering its responses to the Covid-19 pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war and a series of energy price shocks that sent inflation in the European Union above 11% in 2022 and spurred the end of the post-Financial Crisis era of negative interest rates. Lagarde will depart nearly nine months before her term was due to expire in October 2027, while the process to appoint her successor will begin immediately.

items.title: US interest rates held steady and economy grows - what it means for you
items.summary: The Federal Reserve's interest rate decisions affect everything from mortgages to car loans
items.body: The decision comes within a week of the midterm elections and after the central bank raised interest rates for the first time in three years at its September meeting. "The overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgement, is that what we've done in this monetary medicine is starting to work some," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said, referring to September's interest rate rise. Figures published after the Fed's announcement showed the US economy growing at a stronger pace than expected, with inflation running above the Fed's target. An interest rate tells people and businesses how much it costs to borrow money – such as with credit cards, mortgages, or business loans – but also what return they get for saving cash. The Fed influences interest rates in the US through its target range for the federal funds rate, which is the interest rate used by commercial banks for overnight borrowing.

items.title: ‘I earn £126,000 – but nothing’s left at the end of the month’: readers react to the budget
items.summary: From a young chef and a single father to business owners and a pensioner, Guardian readers reveal how John Healey’s measures will affect them What the budget means for you Louie, 24, a chef living in London, says a lot of people have “written off the idea of even considering…
items.body: Louie, 24, a chef living in London , says a lot of people have “written off the idea of even considering getting a property” in their 20s. He is optimistic about the government’s new Your First Home scheme, which will enable people to buy a new-build property with a deposit of just 2.5%, supported by an interest-free equity loan. But he says a smaller deposit alone will not be enough for him. “I’ve found hospitality wages to be far too volatile to even consider saving for a property,” he says. As a result, he is studying an access course with plans to start a physiotherapy degree next year. He hopes that by the time he graduates and gains some experience, he will have a stable enough income and sufficient savings to put down a deposit.

items.title: US moves to lift sanctions on Russia's shadow fleet could undermine Western pressure on Moscow and help fund its war in Ukraine.
items.summary: The US is reportedly considering ways to convert "dark tankers" into legitimate vessels, allowing them to transport crude oil that is not subject to sanctions.
items.body: Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine , Moscow has increasingly relied on a so-called shadow fleet to bypass Western sanctions and transport its oil around the world. Other heavily sanctioned countries, including Iran and Venezuela, have also been accused of using such vessels to export petroleum products . These tankers often rely on deceptive practices like turning off their location transponders to evade detection and conceal the cargo's true origins or destinations. The fleet, which consists largely of aging, uninsured and poorly maintained tankers, has raised widespread concern across the shipping industry. Yet it has expanded rapidly in recent years and now accounts for nearly 19% of global oil tanker capacity, according to estimates by financial intelligence firm S&P Global.

items.title: Ahead of US vote on device testing in mainland China, experts warn of supply chain effects
items.summary: As the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) prepares to vote on Thursday on a proposal to bar device testing in mainland China by 2028, two major American industry associations have warned of potential testing shortages and certification backlogs, given China’s dominance…
items.body: As the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) prepares to vote on Thursday on a proposal to bar device testing in mainland China by 2028, two major American industry associations have warned of potential testing shortages and certification backlogs, given China’s dominance in the sector. Analysts said the proposed restrictions could slow global electronics supply chains and increase costs for manufacturers, particularly American companies that rely heavily on Chinese testing facilities. Under the proposal, laboratories in mainland China would lose their FCC recognition from December 1, 2028, preventing them from carrying out testing required for the US certification of electronic devices such as smartphones and computers. The move has raised concerns among American industry groups.

items.title: Nvidia responds to report Jensen Huang was target of Chinese asset, says diversion allegations were 'investigated and debunked'

items.body: An Nvidia spokesperson on Thursday pushed back on a New York Times report that detailed American intelligence agencies surveilling a person close to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang because they thought she could be a Chinese intelligence asset. According to the Times report , which cited people briefed on intelligence surveillance, Alice Huang, who is linked to the Singapore-based cloud Megaspeed, developed a close relationship with Nvidia's Jensen Huang. Intelligence agencies worried that she was a spy, helping the Chinese government gain information from Nvidia and Jensen Huang, and fretted that Nvidia's CEO had access to President Donald Trump.

items.title: Analysis: Kevin Warsh is keeping Wall Street guessing. It may be his most powerful tool
items.summary: The new chairman made clear he leans toward higher interest rates, but left himself options depending on how the data comes in.
items.body: The Federal Reserve chairman's news conference Wednesday was sharply different from his early appearances in the job, when he often seemed backed into a corner. He's shown he is willing to let the markets guess where he is going — at least to a point. And he has started using his authority to reshape the institution. Warsh was appointed by a president who said cutting interest rates was a litmus test for his choice for Fed chair. When the Federal Open Market Committee opted to hold rates flat in June and July, even with inflation well above the Fed's 2% target, a swarm of commentators questioned the new chairman's credibility. The FOMC's subsequent decision in September to raise rates came with such a hawkish reading of the economy by Warsh that the markets swung sharply in the opposite direction.

items.title: 'Painful' years ahead, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall
items.summary: Budget forecasts show growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt.
items.body: People are facing a "painful" and "depressing" few years ahead, economic think tanks have warned, after forecasts showed growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt. Typical working-age households would see their disposable income fall by £1,050, or 3%, between now and 2029, according to the Resolution Foundation, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the current decade would be the worst for household income growth on record. Chancellor John Healey said his Budget offered "breathing space", but said the government could "never remove completely" cost of living pressures. The UK's official forecaster said its latest economic forecast painted a "pretty grim picture". The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), blamed the difficult financial situation facing the UK on higher borrowing costs and inflation caused by the US-Iran war.

items.title: How £100 vanishes in minutes: inside the ‘slot farms’ targeted in the budget
items.summary: John Healey has hit adult gaming centres with 25% tax. Undercover footage shows how they lure customers The last of five £20 notes disappears into the slot machine as The Verve’s Bittersweet Symphony plays over the shop’s sound system. That’s it, £100 gone in the space of about…
items.body: The last of five £20 notes disappears into the slot machine as The Verve’s Bittersweet Symphony plays over the shop’s sound system. That’s it, £100 gone in the space of about five minutes, swallowed up by one of the many “slot farms” that dominate the shopping streets of Peterborough . All that’s left to show for it is a free KitKat, one of the incentives staff use to tempt customers into staying a little longer and losing a little more. It’s lunchtime on a Thursday and dozens of glassy-eyed hopefuls are having the same experience, feeding in what little cash they have and cursing as it disappears. The same pattern is repeated across the country. Gamblers in Great Britain lost £2.7bn on slot machines last year, nearly double the annual budget of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, which oversees the sector.

items.title: Faisal Islam: This Budget was micro and that was deliberate
items.summary: Chancellor John Healey's plans fall short of radical action to create a promised new economic model.
items.body: It was not a mini Budget, but it was rather small. It might be called the "micro Budget". Small does not necessarily mean bad, but it clearly falls short of radical action to create a promised new economic model. A new "theory of growth" was not unveiled as promised by the prime minister Andy Burnham. It was preamble, roadmap, consultation, perhaps the starter to the main course, which appears to be the PM's 10-year plan next month. It went unsaid, but the clear stategic aim of Healey's statement was to be the "anti-mini Budget". This "steady as she goes" predictable fiscal event set out to avoid the aftermath seen following Liz Truss's mini-budget, in which unexpected and unfunded tax cuts spooked the bond and currency markets.

items.title: ‘There has to be a bolder shift’: retail and hospitality businesses assess relief in budget
items.summary: Chancellor cuts business rates for more small businesses and limits rise in minimum wage for younger workers Budget 2026: key points at a glance “It is like letting the tyres down and then handing you a pump,” says James Nye, assessing the relief handed to businesses in John…
items.body: “It is like letting the tyres down and then handing you a pump,” says James Nye, assessing the relief handed to businesses in John Healey’s first budget as chancellor. The managing director of Norfolk’s Anglian Country Inns argues that the budget made a “couple of steps towards helping” but added more labour costs for already burdened companies. Nye, who employs 500 people at the height of the season at its 10 venues across Norfolk and Hertfordshire, was among those business owners watching Healey carefully on Wednesday, after two previous Labour budgets under Rachel Reeves had loaded extra costs on to businesses. Healey aimed to help high street operators by removing the business rates burden from more small businesses and limiting the rise in the minimum wage for younger workers.

items.title: China’s industrial strength keeps it from ‘turning Japanese’
items.summary: In November 2024, the yield on China’s 30-year government bond fell below its Japanese equivalent for the first time. This was a big deal in financial markets, fanning fears that China’s economy was vulnerable to the type of crisis that condemned Japan to decades of deflation…
items.body: In November 2024, the yield on China’s 30-year government bond fell below its Japanese equivalent for the first time. This was a big deal in financial markets, fanning fears that China’s economy was vulnerable to the type of crisis that condemned Japan to decades of deflation and stagnant growth following the bursting of its asset price bubble in the early 1990s. In November 2025, China’s benchmark 10-year yield followed suit. Although the convergence in the two countries’ bond yields had as much to do with Japan’s success in winning a three-decade battle against deflation, the “Japanification” of China’s economy has been one of the most talked-about themes among economists and investors in the past several years. In a report in August 2023, JPMorgan said there were some eerie similarities between post-property bust China and 1990s Japan.

items.title: Intel stock plunges 21% as chipmaker blames PC slowdown for weak guidance
items.summary: Intel has been a Wall Street darling this year due to its emergence as a player in AI, but the company is being weighed down by a struggling PC market.
items.body: Intel shares plummeted more than 20% in extended trading on Thursday after the chipmaker issued a weak fourth-quarter forecast, citing continued softness in the global PC market. Revenue climbed 21% from $13.7 billion a year earlier, the company said in a press release. However, revenue in Intel's client computing and physical AI group fell 5% from the same quarter a year ago to $8.1 billion, missing estimates, even as data center and AI revenue jumped 78% to $7.3 billion. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier due to soaring costs for memory and other components, according to Counterpoint Research . For the current quarter, Intel said it expects adjusted earnings per share of 25 cents on revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion. Analysts were expecting revenue of $17.1 billion and EPS of 43 cents, according to LSEG.

items.title: 'I live with a ghost' - inside the haunted homes attracting bargain hunters
items.summary: Properties where someone has died in tragic circumstances can have big reductions in price.
items.body: From the moment Ryua first walked into her rental apartment in Tokyo she believed it to be haunted. "When I visited the place for a viewing there was a man standing there, glaring at me," she says. While someone more squeamish would probably have quickly left the flat never to return, Ryua chose to go ahead and move in. "I'm a bit of a contrarian, so I decided I wanted to become friends with this glaring male ghost," adds Ryua, who works as an aidoru, a young entertainer, and who doesn't wish to share her surname. Four years later, and still in the same apartment, she says she continues to experience paranormal activity on a daily basis. She says she hears endless footsteps and the ghost talking. Although Japan has increasingly marked Halloween , external in recent years, many Japanese people take ghosts seriously all year round.

Fresh devolution deals could also be in place following negotiations with leaders in Scotland, Wales and possibly Northern Ireland, allowing the prime minister to say at the next election that he has fulfilled a promise to rewire Britain’s political landscape with a view to giving more local control. This was the message from John Healey’s first budget , which outlined the direction of travel and put in some milestones, including a 2028 commitment to devolve some income tax receipts to mayors of strategic authorities (MSAs). He added the commitment that next year, 20% of business rates revenues will go to mayors.

items.title: Ahead of European talks, Beijing wary of forced yuan appreciation: analysts
items.summary: With top European finance officials expected to meet their Chinese counterparts to push for a stronger yuan, analysts say Beijing remains wary of repeating Japan’s experience after the 1985 Plaza Accord and is likely to reject politically imposed exchange-rate targets. While…
items.body: With top European finance officials expected to meet their Chinese counterparts to push for a stronger yuan, analysts say Beijing remains wary of repeating Japan’s experience after the 1985 Plaza Accord and is likely to reject politically imposed exchange-rate targets. While coordinated Western pressure over China’s large trade surplus and calls for yuan appreciation could intensify, Beijing would probably tolerate gradual, market-driven gains while drawing a firm line to protect its monetary autonomy, they said. David Zhang, a macroeconomics and policy analyst at Trivium China, said Beijing was not opposed to an “orderly appreciation” of the yuan, which could boost its purchasing power and support economic rebalancing, but would “firmly reject any commitment to do so under external pressure”.

items.title: Starbucks sales miss expectations, but its U.S. turnaround is gaining steam

items.body: Starbucks on Thursday reported mixed quarterly results as its international cafes underperformed expectations. However, its U.S. turnaround continues to take hold, as its home market topped expectations during the coffee giant's final quarter of fiscal 2026. "We enter fiscal 2027 with momentum, a clear set of priorities and higher ambitions for what Starbucks can become," CEO Brian Niccol said in a video shared on the company's website. Starbucks is ahead of schedule to meet the fiscal 2028 targets laid out at its investor day in January, he said on the company's earnings conference call. For fiscal 2027, Starbucks is projecting adjusted earnings per share in a range of $3.15 to $3.25, above Wall Street's expectations of earnings per share of $3.14. However, its anticipated revenue decline of 1% is weaker than expected; analysts were forecasting net sales growth of 1.4%.

items.title: Bereaved families will not face tax bill over pension delays under new rules
items.summary: Campaigners had warned some families could face an unfair financial penalty because of delays which were not their fault.
items.body: Bereaved families will no longer be hit by an unexpected tax bill because of severe delays paying out civil service pensions, following a change in Wednesday's Budget. Under previous HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments had to be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free. Campaigners had warned some families could face an unfair financial penalty because of delays which were not their fault. The government has now changed the rules so payments will no longer become taxable solely because more than two years has passed. The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK. Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases.

items.body: The shop workers’ union Usdaw has urged Poundland’s owners to reconsider a decision to prepare the budget chain for administration, putting up to 12,000 jobs at risk. Gordon Brothers filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators to Poundland at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process. The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors for 10 days while a solution to its problems is sought. Gordon Brothers previously rejected a management-backed rescue bid for the discount chain, which operates 600 stores, including Dealz outlets in Ireland. It bought the struggling chain for a nominal £1 from its previous owner, the European retail group Pepco, in June 2025.

items.title: US should spy on Chinese firms to maintain edge in tech race: ex-CIA official
items.summary: A former CIA official has called for Washington to spy on foreign companies to help US firms stay ahead in the technology race, in what would represent a break from long-standing US policy amid intensifying competition with China. “The US lead in many crucial advanced…
items.body: A former CIA official has called for Washington to spy on foreign companies to help US firms stay ahead in the technology race, in what would represent a break from long-standing US policy amid intensifying competition with China. “The US lead in many crucial advanced technologies is being contested or even erased by China,” wrote David Cohen, who served as deputy director of the Central Intelligence Agency under Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden, in an article published by Foreign Affairs earlier this month. “By abstaining from economic espionage, the United States has tilted the playing field against itself and magnified the Chinese threat.” The call for economic espionage, which Cohen claimed could also help counter alleged Chinese efforts to spy on US firms, came as China ramps up efforts to secure its trade secrets.

items.title: Amazon AWS posts 39% revenue growth as cloud rivals also accelerate
items.summary: Amazon's cloud signed deals with Meta and OpenAI during the quarter, helping revenue to exceed consensus.
items.body: Amazon's cloud-computing unit reported more rapid third-quarter growth than analysts had projected. Revenue came in at $45.98 billion, up 39% year over year and above the $45.29 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount, according to a statement . Growth in the second quarter came in at about 37% . "Our core compute and storage revenue grew at their fastest rates in several years," Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on a conference call with analysts. The AWS growth rate was the highest since the fourth quarter of 2021. Amazon remains the top cloud by revenue, but growth has also sped up at rivals Alphabet and Microsoft. On Wednesday Alphabet said the Google Cloud business, which contains infrastructure and Google Workspace subscriptions, more than doubled in the third quarter.

items.body: He announced £100 energy payment for millions and a tax rise on banks, among other measures. BBC News has been speaking to people on a range of incomes on how they feel about their finances and how the Budget affects them. Dave Herbert is a professional driver on £30,000 a year. He moves cars between showrooms and does deliveries and says fuel prices have been "crazy" this year. He spends around £350 a month on petrol for work and personal use. That's 40% to 50% more than at the start of the year, he says. He has to commute into Cardiff, a 62-mile round trip from his home in Ynysddu. "I'd love to have a hybrid car but even an entry-level used car is too expensive." The 48-year-old, who is married with a 12-year-old daughter, says he has to find the extra money for fuel "from an already tight budget" and "dreads" filling up at the pump.

items.summary: E-commerce company posts high cloud computing sales but gives a cautious sales forecast for the fourth quarter Amazon offered a mixed picture of its financial health on Thursday in its quarterly earnings report. The e-commerce company gave a cautious sales forecast for the…
items.body: Amazon offered a mixed picture of its financial health on Thursday in its quarterly earnings report. The e-commerce company gave a cautious sales forecast for the current fourth quarter, which encompasses the critical holiday shopping period, after delivering fiscal third-quarter results that came in below Wall Street analysts’ expectations. The Seattle-based company posted strong growth, however, in its prominent cloud computing unit. Sales in its cloud computing unit, called AWS, rose 39.3% during the latest quarter ended 30 September, higher than the 37% clip in the previous quarter. It marked the fastest growth rate in nearly five years, the company said. Still, shares were down more than 6% in after-market trading when the results were released as investors focused on the core business.

items.title: Billionaire Ambani cries tears of joy as Jio Platforms becomes the second most valued Indian firm

items.body: Billionaire Mukesh Ambani has become the owner of the two most valued companies in India, after a stellar listing of Jio Platforms , the country's largest telecom operator and digital services firm. The share of Jio Platforms continued to climb higher on Thursday, opening 3.3% higher a day after its market debut. The Meta - and Google -backed company listed on Wednesday at a premium of over 25% to its IPO price, leading to a market capitalization of 13.05 trillion rupees ($137.1 billion). Ambani's flagship company, Reliance Industries , also the most valued company in India, owns more than a 64% stake in Jio Platforms after the initial public offering. Ahead of the listing, the patriarch of the Ambani family teared up as his three children shared the journey of building Jio and vowed to create value for investors over the next 50 years.

items.summary: Instacart shoppers will be able to buy from 150,000 stores, compared to the 100,000 currently available on the platform, the firms said.
items.body: DoorDash will acquire grocery delivery firm Instacart in a $17bn (£12.8bn) deal, creating a behemoth that will bring more meals, quick-need purchases and big weekly shops directly to customers. DoorDash said the deal, expected to be final in about a year, will expand options for customers and let more sellers use the companies' services. Instacart shoppers will be able to buy from 150,000 stores, up from the current 100,000, while DoorDash will reach beyond restaurants into retail, the firms said. "Together, we can accelerate innovation across the grocery industry and make online grocery more seamless and affordable for the millions of households we serve," Instacart's chief executive said.

items.title: Nvidia CEO reportedly targeted by an alleged Chinese spy
items.summary: Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by an alleged Chinese spy who had done business with him, according…
items.body: US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by an alleged Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to a new report by the New York Times. Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China , prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources. In the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times.

items.title: It's a 'socialist' bank — and North Dakota Republicans love it
items.summary: Democratic socialist candidates have held up North Dakota's state-owned bank as a model to emulate.
items.body: BISMARCK, N.D. — In 1918, an offshoot of the progressive farmer-labor movement known as the Nonpartisan League swept into power in North Dakota , riding a populist groundswell of anger directed at big banks and industry barons in Minneapolis and Chicago. The group was organized by former Socialist Party member Arthur C. Townley, a failed flax farmer who barnstormed the state in a borrowed Ford Model T calling for public ownership of key industries, including banks, mills and factories. By 1919, the state legislature authorized a state-owned and -operated bank. Over a century later, the Bank of North Dakota still stands, and the state is reaping the benefits. The Bank of North Dakota is the nation's only surviving state-owned and -operated bank.

items.body: Seven oil tankers carrying an estimated 288,000 tonnes of Russian diesel are now sailing towards the US, though it is uncertain if the vessels will be able to unload amid a political row about the legality of the shipments. The transport, tracked by the pressure group Greenpeace , is the first phase of a contentious supply deal negotiated between presidents Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin earlier this month, reversing years of sanctions on Russia oil. Previous reports had counted three tankers that had departed Russian oil terminals in the Baltic Sea, but using a range of sources, including shipping tracking websites, Greenpeace believes its monitoring exercise is the most complete yet.

The electric vehicle maker also revised its 2026 guidance to mark expected improvements in its vehicle deliveries, pre-tax adjusted earnings and capital expenditures. The new guidance calls for a pre-tax adjusted loss of between $1.75 billion and $1.85 billion — a $100 million improvement at the midpoint from its prior guidance — vehicle deliveries of between 67,000 and 70,000 units, up from at least 65,000; and capital expenditures of between $1.4 billion and $1.5 billion, $300 million less at the midpoint.

items.summary: ‘Compliance managers’ to have discussions with authority’s wealthiest customers in attempt to raise tax revenues Business live – latest updates The UK’s tax authority is assigning dedicated “customer compliance managers” to more than 200 billionaires as part of a crackdown meant…
items.body: The UK’s tax authority is assigning dedicated “customer compliance managers” to more than 200 billionaires as part of a crackdown meant to raise £500m for the public purse. HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) said it had for the first time compiled a list of billionaires who are required to pay tax in the UK, regardless of whether they formally live in the country, to tackle a “wealthy tax gap” caused by those who do not pay what they ought. In an announcement after Wednesday’s budget, the authority said it was allocating a customer compliance manager (CCM) to each billionaire with a UK tax footprint, whose complex tax affairs are often hard for HMRC to manage. “Billionaires can present a particular example of this, with affairs often spanning multiple taxes, entities and jurisdictions and a greater need for early and coordinated engagement,” HMRC said.

items.body: Christine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, has said she is stepping down nine months early to speak her mind about world affairs and confront the “misrepresentation of the truth”. Ending months of speculation about her future at the European Central Bank , Lagarde said she would quit her role as president in March rather than October next year because the rules of neutrality that governed her job prevented her from influencing debate about financial and economics affairs. She spoke at the end of a press conference to explain the ECB’s decision to hold interest rates – maintaining its key deposit rate at 2.5% – despite inflation climbing to 3.8% last month, its highest since September 2023.

items.body: Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has summoned water industry bosses to Whitehall after a report found that the environmental performance of the big companies has worsened despite investment. “People are sick of excuses,” Dame Angela said, after the Environment Agency joined the Drinking Water Inspectorate, Natural Resources Wales and Ofwat for a joint report that rated eight of the nine water companies in England as “poor” or “requiring improvement”. There were 74 serious pollution incidents, the category that causes significant harm to the environment, the report said. That was just one fewer than the previous year, despite billions of pounds of investment, bans on bosses’ bonuses and a public outcry.

Elon Musk is a "real genius", Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday after revealing the two are in "close" contact about satellite technology. The remarks came during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, during which Putin discussed Russia's own satellite internet project Rassvet, which provides internet connections to people from satellites. "He's a genius, a real genius," Putin said of Musk, according to a translation of his remarks by the BBC. "We are in close contact with our American partners, including Mr. Musk." Starlink is part of Musk's company SpaceX. The company did not respond to a request for comment. Putin added that it was important for Russia to be in contact with Musk so Rassvet and Starlink satellites do not "interfere with each other in orbit".

items.title: Is this play-safe budget a sign that the prime minister is planning an early election? | Larry Elliott
items.summary: There’s no real strategy behind this hotchpotch of measures. Andy Burnham may be parking the big decisions until he has a true mandate Continue reading...
items.body: G reat hopes were invested in Andy Burnham when he became prime minister in July. He went big on the failings of 40 years of neoliberalism, emphasised the need for Britain to start making things again and promised growth in every postcode . Back in the summer, John Healey’s first budget was seen as an opportunity to start delivering on these ambitions, but it has been clear for some time that it wouldn’t do so. The road to the New Jerusalem – judging by the chancellor’s “ breathing space ” package – will be a slow and arduous one. Healey has taken what he inherited from Rachel Reeves and performed some minor tweaks. Not so much a revolution as continuity Keir Starmer.

items.title: Hegseth reportedly fires U.S. top military planner as Trump downplays Iran peace talks
items.summary: Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
items.body: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has reportedly fired the Pentagon's top military planner amid concerns that Washington may restart strikes on Iran after the midterm elections. Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Staff, according to the Associated Press . No reason was given for his dismissal, and nobody was named as his replacement. Sylvia has now retired, ABC News reported , citing two people familiar with the matter. The AP also reported that U.S. officials have told some countries in the Middle East to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week's midterm elections , as well as for any Iranian retaliation.

items.title: GoTo's ride-hailing earnings drop on Indonesia driver commission cap
items.body: JAKARTA -- Indonesia's GoTo Group on Thursday said its core ride-hailing and delivery business profit dropped 25% in the July-September period from the previous quarter due to a driver commission cap rule that took effect on July 1.

items.title: The ‘breathing space budget’ – breathing space for the government, that is | John Crace
items.summary: John Healey aced the morning-after media round because his Martin Lewis measures left nothing to challenge him on Maybe it had been one of the greatest acts of political genius after all. The day after the budget is usually the moment when things start to fall apart. When…
items.body: M aybe it had been one of the greatest acts of political genius after all. The day after the budget is usually the moment when things start to fall apart. When clued-up journalists and economists have had a chance to go through all the fine points the chancellor would rather everyone had missed. The forecasts that suggest everything is predicated on a wing and a prayer. The hidden unfunded tax cuts. The greater-than-expected spending commitments. But on Thursday morning Andy Burnham and John Healey could afford themselves a sigh of relief. All had gone about as well as they could have hoped. It turns out that when you don’t make any massive tax or spending commitments , there isn’t a great deal to unravel. All there had been was a raft of small-scale interventions designed to help people with their personal finances. Call it the Martin Lewis budget .

items.title: Komatsu lifts profit outlook on construction, mining demand in Americas
items.body: TOKYO -- Heavy equipment maker Komatsu expects net profit in the fiscal year ending March 2027 to rise 1% on the year to 382 billion yen ($2.42 billion), the company said Thursday, upgrading its earlier forecast on stronger-than-expected sales of construction machinery in North and Latin America.

items.title: Burnham promised big change – where was it? Instead we got the Martin Lewis budget | Aditya Chakrabortty
items.summary: The financial guru’s fingerprints are all over John Healey’s red book – but Lewis is not a politician. His everyday fixes can’t meet this turbulent moment Was this Andy Burnham’s budget – the bold vision of a new prime minister who burns with a passion to topple “40 years of…
items.body: W as this Andy Burnham’s budget – the bold vision of a new prime minister who burns with a passion to topple “40 years of neoliberalism”? Fat chance. Was it John Healey’s budget – the repair job of a cautious chancellor fretting about record-high taxes, £3tn of public debt and an economy stuck in first gear? Little sign of that. This budget was cast in the image of a man who isn’t in Burnham’s government or even a Labour politician – but who appears almost every day on TV, on podcasts and is probably better known than 649 of the MPs at Westminster. Today’s budget was the Martin Lewis budget. Lewis is the MoneySavingExpert , whose weekly Money Tips email advises 10 million British subscribers on cheap mortgages, Black Friday deals and how to score two pizzas for £10. Tips and tricks to stave off rising prices and make the most of the money you have.

items.title: Norwegian shares surge 13% on earnings beat, guidance raise
items.summary: Norwegian said the company's bookings had "improved modestly" but remain below its optimal range.
items.body: Shares of Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings surged 13% Thursday after the company posted better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and raised its outlook for the full year. The cruise line reported third-quarter revenue of $2.95 billion, topping Wall Street expectations of $2.88 billion, according to analyst estimates from LSEG. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization was $937 million, which exceeded Norwegian's previous guidance of $874 million. Adjusted EPS was $1.12, exceeding previous guidance of 90 cents and outpacing analysts' expectations of 94 cents, per LSEG. Norwegian also raised its full-year guidance, citing its stronger-than-expected third-quarter performance. The company now expects 2026 adjusted EBITDA of $2.55 billion and adjusted EPS of about $1.70.
